The Soviets notably included Ukraine and were being invaded in a genocidal war of conquest. Wildberries strikes are not about forcing some total victory. They are about harming the consumer economy of a country engaged in a war of choice that could end the war at any time. For Ukraine, this war is existential. For Russia, it is not. If the Russian economy suffers and they are unable to reliably gain ground, that provides compounding pressure on the Russian government to end the war. After reading much of the commentary on the Mecca Agreement, I don't believe the superficial institutional similarities are sufficient to justify comparisons to NATO. And the agreement does not represent an anti-Western or anti-Eastern alignment. It is better understood as a regional framework designed to stabilize the immediate strategic environment. The agreement's unique combination of capabilities is what makes it stand out. Turkey contributes strong land forces and a mature defense industrial base; Saudi Arabia provides significant financial resources and air-power capability; and Pakistan adds a nuclear deterrent dimension. This combination gives the arrangement the potential to carry more strategic weight than many previous regional security initiatives. From a technical standpoint, the parties' power profiles are primarily complementary rather than redundant. As a result, the agreement's deterrence architecture appears more integrated and potentially scalable than comparable regional groupings. However, it would be premature to assign it a large geopolitical mission or to make assumptions about outcomes that have yet to occur. The agreement's long-term significance will be determined less by its headline ambitions than by its members' ability to translate complementary capabilities into sustained institutional and strategic cooperation.
